paragraphs.source_en: At the 1884-1885 Berlin Conference, also known as the Congo Conference, which legitimated foreign colonialism in Africa, the Ottoman delegation referred to its holdings of Tripoli, Benghazi, and Ghat in Libya as colonies. Writing in 1908, an Ottoman administrator and parliamentarian criticised Ottoman neglect of North Africa and advocated a revitalised Ottoman commitment to Tripoli. His reason was explicitly imperial. Controlling Tripoli allowed ‘the fastest civilised connecting link’ between Europe and the markets of Central Africa.’ In his 1909 travelogue of the Sudan, a diplomat bemoaned the fact that the Ottomans had not acted in time to colonise that country, ceding it to another colonial power, the British.
